strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation on seven medical QA benchmarks with 12 baselines, showing consistent gains over strong test-time scaling and RAG methods (e.g., +6.8 average accuracy over Qwen3-8B and +5.3 over the strongest RAG baseline TC-RAG).
The ablation study cleanly separates the contributions of multi-round refinement, the conflict-guided Retrieval Agent, and the Ranking Agent, with each component yielding measurable gains.
The test-time scaling analysis over refinement rounds T, candidate pool size N, and backbone scale (8B to 32B) provides useful practical guidance and demonstrates scalability.
The paper is largely reproducible: prompt templates, retrieval configuration, evaluator training details, and hyperparameters are provided, and code is stated to be available.
The proposed conflict-guided retrieval is well motivated and addresses a real limitation of token-level uncertainty signals in medical RAG, where models can hallucinate with high confidence.
The limitations and impact statement honestly discuss inference cost, corpus coverage, evaluator quality, and risks of medical deployment.
The additional analyses (query granularity K, Best-of-N comparison, compatibility with SR-RAG, oracle upper bound) enrich the empirical picture and clarify the method's behavior.
weaknesses: The central claim that semantic conflict is a superior retrieval signal to token-level uncertainty is not directly isolated. There is no ablation that replaces conflict-guided queries with token-level uncertainty queries inside the same multi-round framework; comparisons to FLARE and TC-RAG confound many design differences.

The theoretical grounding in boosting and adaptive self-consistency is largely analogical. No formal residual minimization or boosting-style weighting is implemented, and the proposed confidence threshold epsilon is not used in Algorithm 1 or the experiments, which rely on fixed T. Thus the 'adaptive scaling' claim is not empirically supported.

The Ranking Agent's claim of mitigating long-context degradation is not directly tested. There is no measurement of lost-in-the-middle behavior, no control for random/reverse/truncated history ordering, and no ablation of document ordering. The gain may simply come from including quality scores or selecting high-quality candidates.

Statistical rigor is limited: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed variance are reported. Several benchmarks are small (e.g., MedExpQA 125, MedBullets 308), and some per-dataset gains are modest, making it difficult to judge robustness.

The external evaluator is trained on benchmark-specific training splits and Qwen3-8B generated reasoning traces. For the Qwen3-32B experiments, it is unclear whether the evaluator is retrained or transferred, and the reliance on ground-truth labels may limit real-world applicability.

There is an inconsistency between Algorithm 1, which resets the document context D_{t+1} to empty each round, and the text claiming the evidence pool is continuously updated. The hybrid-context experiment also suggests a warm start, so the exact document accumulation policy is unclear.
Notation is inconsistent: Appendix D uses N for the maximum refinement round, while the main text uses N for candidate pool size and T for rounds, which can confuse reproduction.

Retrieval and conflict-resolution quality are never evaluated directly; only end-task accuracy is reported. It is not shown whether the generated queries actually target the correct knowledge gaps or whether the conflict signal correlates with retrieval success.

The 'agentic' framework is primarily prompt engineering plus a BERT/ModernBERT evaluator, with no tool use beyond retrieval. Relative to existing multi-round RAG, verifier-based selection, and conflict-aware RAG work, the technical novelty is moderate.

The abstract and introduction overclaim a general 'boosting' and 'consensus' mechanism, but the method is evaluated only on multiple-choice medical QA and not on open-ended clinical reasoning or decision support, limiting the scope of the conclusions.

strengths: Well-motivated problem and a clearly described framework: three specialized agents (Solver, Retrieval, Ranking) with an explicit state transition S_t -> S_{t+1}, pseudocode, and a coherent narrative around using semantic conflict to steer retrieval.

Broad and consistent empirical evaluation: 7 medical Q&A benchmarks, 12 baselines spanning backbones, test-time scaling, naive RAG, and adaptive RAG, plus an ablation on Qwen3-8B and a replication on Qwen3-32B. The gains are directionally consistent across datasets and model scales.
Clean component ablation (Table 2) and test-time scaling analysis (Table 3) that isolate the Retrieval and Ranking Agents and characterize behavior w.r.t. rounds T and candidate pool N.

Reproducibility effort is above average: identical MedCorp corpus, BM25 retriever, and MedCPT reranker across RAG baselines, plus appendix details on prompts, retrieval configuration, verifier training data/architecture/hyperparameters.
Honest limitations and impact statements acknowledging inference cost, corpus coverage limits, and the dependence on imperfect quality estimators.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the paper largely composes existing ingredients—self-consistency sampling, adaptive/iterative RAG, multi-round self-refinement, and verifier/entropy reranking. The novel element (conflict-guided querying plus history re-ranking) is incremental and not clearly distinguished from prior adaptive RAG work.

The 'theoretical grounding in classic principles' (Sec. 3.5) is only an analogy to boosting and self-consistency. There is no formal analysis, convergence argument, or bound; framing this as a theoretical contribution overstates what is actually a qualitative metaphor.

The central claim—that semantic conflict is a better retrieval signal than token-level uncertainty—is never directly tested. There is no ablation contrasting conflict-driven queries against a generic question-derived query or query rewriting, so the mechanism is asserted rather than validated.

Internally inconsistent use of signals: the paper criticizes token-level uncertainty as noisy, yet MA-RAG-int uses sequence-level entropy as its ranking score, and MA-RAG-hyb combines it with the verifier without resolving the tension.

MA-RAG-ext depends on a ModernBERT verifier fine-tuned on the same benchmark distributions (MedQA, MedMCQA, MedExpQA, and a re-split MedXpertQA). This injects supervised, in-domain signal that baselines do not receive, blurring the 'test-time scaling' framing and likely inflating the reported MA-RAG-ext advantage; the comparison is not supervision- or budget-matched.

No statistical rigor: results appear to be single-run point estimates with no seeds, error bars, or confidence intervals. Several reported deltas (e.g., ~1-2 points between MA-RAG-int and MA-RAG-ext, and the T=4 vs T=8 gap) are plausibly within noise, undermining claims of 'consistent superiority'.

Compute and data budgets are not equalized across methods (e.g., SC uses 20 paths; MA-RAG uses N candidates over T rounds; MA-RAG additionally uses a trained verifier and a custom MedXpertQA split). The headline '+6.8 points over the backbone' compares against the base model rather than the strongest baseline, and the '37% improvement on MedXpertQA' is a relative figure on very low absolute accuracy (~22%), which also raises questions about the evaluation setup on that dataset.

Baseline coverage omits prominent multi-round/agentic RAG approaches (e.g., Self-RAG, IRCoT-style interleaved retrieval) that are the most natural competitors, making the claim of surpassing 'competitive RAG baselines' incomplete.

strengths: Addresses an important and safety-critical problem: reliable medical question answering with retrieval, mitigating hallucinations and outdated knowledge.

Proposes a clear and reasonably well-motivated multi-agent framework (Solver, Retrieval, Ranking) that uses semantic conflict among sampled responses as a retrieval trigger and ranks reasoning traces to mitigate long-context degradation.

Extensive empirical evaluation: seven medical benchmarks, twelve baselines, two backbone scales (Qwen3-8B/32B), ablations of retrieval and ranking, test-time scaling w.r.t. T and N, query granularity, compatibility with SR-RAG, comparison to Best-of-N, and an Oracle ranking upper bound.

Reports substantial average gains (+6.8 over backbone, +5.3 over strongest RAG baseline, +37% relative on MedXpertQA), with MA-RAG-ext generally outperforming MA-RAG-int, supporting the utility of the learned verifier.

Reproducibility is largely strong: pseudocode, agent prompts, corpus/retriever/reranker details, evaluator training data/architecture/hyperparameters, and implementation settings are provided; code availability is indicated.
Limitations and broader impact are discussed honestly, including inference cost, corpus coverage, verifier imperfection, and clinical deployment risks.
weaknesses: No statistical significance analysis: no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or paired tests. Several benchmarks are small (MedExpQA 125, MedBullets 308), so 1-2 point differences may be noise; claims of consistent superiority are not fully established.

Compute fairness is not fully controlled. Main MA-RAG uses up to T=8 rounds x N=8 candidates plus retrieval and a fine-tuned verifier, while some baselines (e.g., SC with 20 paths, adaptive RAG) are not compute-matched; the paper lacks token/FLOP/latency accounting. Although Multi-Refine is matched, broader comparisons conflate compute with method gains.

The theoretical grounding in self-consistency and boosting is an informal analogy rather than formal analysis; no convergence guarantee, no specified or ablated gating threshold epsilon, and no evidence that the 'boosting residual' framing yields algorithmic benefits.

Conflict-guided retrieval is not independently validated: the paper does not quantify conflict quality, retrieval recall/precision, or whether identified conflicts correspond to true knowledge gaps. The early termination rule may stop when the model is confidently wrong (consistent but incorrect).

The ranking evaluator is trained on Qwen3-8B-generated responses and then used for ranking; potential distribution shift when applied to Qwen3-32B and limited robustness analysis. Ranking gains are modest (+1.6 avg), and MA-RAG-ext underperforms the Extrinsic Recall@2 oracle (62.2 vs 63.0).

Presentation and reference quality need improvement: numerous citation mismatches (e.g., Guu et al. 2020 listed as Guo et al. 2025; DeepSeek-R1 year mismatch; MedBullets cited as Chen et al. 2024 vs 2025a), typos ('Grattafori', 'inferent-time'), incomplete code URL, Appendix D confusingly states N=8 for maximum rounds, and main results use T=8 while the text recommends T=4.

Missing comparisons and analyses: no comparison to more recent agentic/multi-agent RAG or verifier-based medical test-time scaling methods; no benchmark contamination discussion; case studies promised but not shown in main text; no detailed failure-mode analysis.

Ablation of ranking does not fully isolate ranking from additional context or score presentation; the hybrid ranking gives little gain, and the gap to the Oracle (62.2 vs 69.6) indicates current quality estimators are still weak.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 7 diverse medical Q&A benchmarks, 13 baselines spanning four paradigms (backbones, test-time scaling, naive RAG, adaptive RAG, multi-agent), with controlled RAG infrastructure (identical MedCorp corpus, BM25 retriever, MedCPT reranker) to ensure fair comparison.

Well-motivated core idea: using high-level semantic conflict among candidate responses as a retrieval trigger is an intuitive and interpretable alternative to noisy token-level uncertainty, and the paper provides both quantitative LLM-as-a-judge validation (Table 18) and qualitative case studies to support this premise.

Clean ablation study (Table 2) that isolates the incremental contributions of multi-round refinement, the retrieval agent, and the ranking agent, plus a useful attribution analysis (Table 14) showing gains are not merely due to the trained evaluator.

Thorough secondary analyses: test-time scaling w.r.t. rounds T and pool size N (Table 3, Fig. 5, Table 10), scalability to Qwen3-32B (Table 4), efficiency comparison (Tables 5, 17), robustness across independent runs (Table 16), and compatibility with existing RAG pipelines (Table 15).
Reproducibility is reasonably strong: detailed prompt templates, evaluator training data construction and hyperparameters (Tables 7, 8), retrieval configuration, and claimed code release.
Honest and specific limitations discussion covering inference cost, corpus coverage, and imperfect quality estimation.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical grounding' in classical boosting (Sec. 3.5) is analogical rather than formal; no theorem, convergence guarantee, or formal connection is established, so the boosting/self-consistency framing adds limited technical substance beyond motivation.

Novelty is largely compositional: the framework combines self-consistency sampling, adaptive/conflict-driven retrieval, and history re-ranking. Each component exists in prior work, and the conflict-as-signal and ranking ideas are intuitive extensions rather than a fundamentally new method.

The extrinsic evaluator is trained on data drawn from four of the seven evaluated benchmarks (MedQA, MedMCQA, MedExpQA, MedXpertQA), making it in-domain for the majority of test sets. Although train/test splits are disjoint, this overlap is not adequately discussed and could inflate the reported MA-RAG-ext gains relative to genuinely out-of-domain settings.

The ranking agent's benefit is modest and inconsistent: MA-RAG-ext only exceeds MA-RAG-int by 1.2 points on average, and MA-RAG-int is actually higher on MMLU-Pro (70.9 vs 70.7) and NEJM (60.8 vs 60.5). This weakens the claimed importance of the ranking module.

Inference cost is high (e.g., 12,762 generated tokens and ~12.6x base wall-clock on MedXpertQA), and the 'favorable cost-performance trade-off' claim is somewhat generous; the paper does not report a full compute-matched comparison against SC/Best-of-N.
Some results are non-monotonic (e.g., Medbullets N=4 degrades from Round 2 to Round 3) and this instability is not analyzed, leaving the convergence/termination dynamics underexplored.

Claims such as the '37% relative improvement on MedXpertQA' are technically accurate but sit on the benchmark that is partly used for evaluator training, so the headline generalization claim should be tempered.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: 7 medical benchmarks, 13 baselines spanning 5 paradigms, two backbone scales (Qwen3-8B/32B), plus ablations, robustness (4-run std dev), efficiency, and compatibility analyses.
Reproducibility effort is substantial: code release (claimed), detailed appendix with prompt templates, retrieval configs, evaluator training details, and dataset statistics.

The core intuition—using high-level semantic conflict among sampled responses as a retrieval trigger instead of noisy token-level uncertainty—is intuitive, interpretable, and qualitatively illustrated with case studies.

Clear, well-organized presentation with informative figures (score-density plots, scaling curves) and an honest limitations section covering latency, corpus coverage, and imperfect quality estimators.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. Conflict-aware retrieval (Choi et al., 2025), multi-round/adaptive RAG (FLARE, DRAGIN, TC-RAG), verifier-based reranking, and multi-agent refinement are all pre-existing ideas; the paper combines them without a fundamentally new mechanism. The 'agentic' framing largely renames standard multi-round retrieval plus reranking.

The 'Theoretical Grounding' (Sec. 3.5) is rhetorical rather than rigorous. The boosting analogy ('semantic conflict as residual', 'gradient direction', 'weak-to-strong learner') is asserted with no formal definition, objective, bound, or proof, and the self-consistency link is likewise loose. Presenting this as theory overclaims.

Attribution of gains is weak. The largest jump in the ablation is from Multi-Refine (+3.3), which is the non-novel multi-round self-refinement baseline; the marginal contributions of the retrieval agent (+1.9) and ranking agent (+1.6) are modest and plausibly within sampling noise (only 4 datasets are variance-tested, and per-dataset ranking gains are sometimes flat, e.g., MedQA 77.1→77.1). The headline '+6.8 over backbone' compares against the weakest reference rather than the strongest non-novel baseline.

The '+37% relative improvement' claim is inconsistent: 22.2 vs backbone 16.1 is ~38% relative, but 22.2 vs the best baseline (MDAgents/TC-RAG ~18.2) is only ~22%. The abstract/intro framing conflates these.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable. Compute budgets are not matched (SC uses 20 paths; MA-RAG uses N=8 over multiple rounds with retrieval; MA-RAG generates ~12.8k tokens vs SC ~10k but also retrieves). Baselines (FLARE, TC-RAG, MDAgents) are reimplemented under a different backbone, which may not reflect their intended performance.

Stability concern: the T ablation is non-monotonic on Medbullets (T=2: 60.4 > T=4: 59.1), and the paper recommends T=4 while reporting T=8 in main results, undercutting the 'convergence to stable consensus' narrative.

The extrinsic evaluator is a domain-fine-tuned ModernBERT trained on medical QA data; its advantage over entropy (+1.2) may reflect domain supervision rather than the agentic framework, and the paper's own gap analysis shows the ranking agent is far from the Oracle (62.2 vs 69.6), i.e., quality estimation is a major unresolved bottleneck.

The LLM-as-a-Judge validation (Appendix G) relies on models named 'Qwen3.6 Plus', 'DeepSeek V3.2', and 'MiniMax M2.7', which are not identifiable/verifiable. This makes the central premise validation (that conflicts are genuine and queries are faithful) hard to trust.

The code link is incomplete ('Our code is available at'), and key implementation choices (e.g., how NEJM multi-answer questions interact with majority voting over single-answer candidates) are underspecified, limiting reliable reproduction.

strengths: Proposes MA-RAG, a well-motivated agentic RAG framework that uses semantic conflict among sampled candidate responses as a retrieval signal and ranks history traces to mitigate long-context degradation.
Extensive empirical evaluation on seven medical Q&A benchmarks with 13 baselines, two backbone scales (8B and 32B), ablations, test-time scaling analysis, efficiency analysis, and robustness checks.
Fair RAG comparison setup: all RAG-based methods use the same MedCorp corpus, BM25 retriever, and MedCPT reranker, which strengthens the validity of RAG-specific comparisons.
Detailed appendix with prompt templates, retrieval configurations, evaluator training details, case studies, and additional analyses, supporting reproducibility.
Demonstrates substantial and consistent improvements, especially on challenging benchmarks such as MedXpertQA, and shows lower variance across runs than several baselines.
Provides both intrinsic and extrinsic ranking variants, with the extrinsic evaluator yielding clear gains, and includes an oracle upper-bound analysis to contextualize the ranking component.
Discusses limitations and broader impact honestly, including inference cost and corpus dependence.
weaknesses: The central claim that semantic conflict is a better retrieval signal is not directly ablated: there is no comparison of conflict-guided query generation against alternative query strategies (e.g., question-only queries, entropy-based queries, or random query expansion). The ablation only shows that adding a retrieval agent helps, not that conflict guidance is the key driver.

The extrinsic evaluator (MA-RAG-ext) is trained on Qwen3-8B outputs and on training splits of several evaluation domains. For MedXpertQA, the authors create a custom 4:1 split and train the evaluator on 4/5 of the benchmark, raising concerns about in-domain leakage and comparability to public results. Main-table comparisons of MA-RAG-ext against baselines without the evaluator may overstate gains, though Appendix F.5 partially addresses this.

The theoretical grounding in boosting is informal and not rigorously established. There is no formal residual minimization or convergence guarantee, and the empirical results show saturation and occasional non-monotonicity (e.g., Medbullets T=2 to T=4), which weakens the boosting analogy.

Novelty is moderate: the method largely combines existing ideas such as self-consistency, adaptive RAG, conflict-aware retrieval, and LLM-based reranking. The contribution is more of a well-engineered integration than a fundamentally new methodology.

Several benchmarks are small (e.g., MedExpQA has 125 questions, Medbullets 308), so reported gains may have high variance. Only a limited 4-run robustness analysis is provided, and no statistical significance tests are reported.

Inference cost is high: MA-RAG-ext generates ~12.8k tokens and takes ~70.7s per question on MedXpertQA, roughly 12x the base model. The claim of a favorable cost-performance trade-off is plausible against MDAgents but may still be impractical for real-time clinical deployment.

Reproducibility is potentially limited by the missing code link in the provided manuscript ('Our code is available at' with no URL) and by the custom MedXpertQA split, which would need to be released to reproduce the exact evaluation.

The conflict signal is derived from the same LLM's samples; if all candidates share the same hallucination, no conflict is detected and retrieval is not triggered. The paper does not analyze this failure mode or its frequency.

The extrinsic evaluator's generalizability to other backbones or medical domains is not fully tested; experiments focus on Qwen3-8B/32B, and the evaluator is trained specifically on Qwen3-8B reasoning traces.
Some strong recent agentic RAG baselines (e.g., Self-RAG, CRAG) are not compared, so the empirical comparison, while broad, may not reflect the strongest current alternatives.
